title: Notes from E-Marking Centre on SSC-I Computer Science Examination May 2018
subject: Computer Science
introduction: This document has been produced for the teachers and candidates of Secondary School Certificate (SSC-I) Computer Science. It contains comments on candidates' responses to the 2018 SSC-I Examination, indicating the quality of the responses and highlighting their relative strengths and weaknesses, along with complete 2025 Syllabus SLO mappings and solved model answers.
generalObservations: In general, questions related to types of computers (Q.6a), CPU components & system buses (Q.6b), input devices / mouse events (Q.2b), types of application software (Q.7a), MS PowerPoint chart datasheets (Q.4c), and MS Word change case (Q.4b) were well attempted.

Questions based on the historical evolution of computers (Q.1), memory unit conversions (Q.2a), Windows Start menu keyboard shortcuts (Q.4a), octal-to-decimal fractional conversions (Q.3a), user interface definitions (Q.5a), and Disk Operating System (DOS) commands (Q.5b) required further practice.

questions.questionText:
Names of some computing devices that were invented during the evolution of computer are given below:
• `ENIAC` • `UNIVAC` • `Mark-1` • `Abacus` • `Difference engine` • `Punch card tabulator` • `Analytical engine` • `Pascal's Pascaline calculator`

Choose appropriate name from the list inside the box and write it with corresponding statement about a computing device. *(Note: Only one name can be used for one statement.)* (5 Marks)
**i.** `_________________________` was steam powered, fully automatic and could print the results as well.
**ii.** `_________________________` works on decimal arithmetic rather than binary arithmetic.
**iii.** `_________________________` was a general purpose, fully program-controlled and automatic mechanical digital computer.
**iv.** `_________________________` had a system of gears. One-tooth gear of this machine engages tooth with a ten-tooth gear once every time it revolves.
**v.** `_________________________` processes data in numerical form using digital circuits.
questions.currentTopic: Out of 2025 Syllabus (Legacy Evolution of Computers)
questions.sloText: Describe the brief history and evolution of computing devices (Abacus, Pascaline, Difference Engine, Analytical Engine, Tabulating Machine, Mark-I, ENIAC, UNIVAC);
checkingHints: 1 mark for each correct computing device matched to its statement: i. Difference engine, ii. ENIAC, iii. Analytical engine, iv. Pascal's Pascaline calculator, v. Mark-1 (5 × 1 = 5 Marks).
questions.overallPerformance: Most of the responses for this question performed below average.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses showed good understanding of the evolution of computers and wrote the correct terms (Difference engine, ENIAC, Analytical engine, Pascal's Pascaline calculator, Mark-1) to complete all five statements.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses identified Difference engine and/or Pascal's Pascaline calculator, but randomly guessed Abacus or Punch card tabulator for the remaining statements.
suggestions: Create a chronological timeline chart comparing the key mechanism and inventor of each historical computing device.
questions.modelAnswer:
**i.** **`Difference engine`** was steam powered, fully automatic and could print the results as well. *(Invented by Charles Babbage in 1822)*
**ii.** **`ENIAC`** works on decimal arithmetic rather than binary arithmetic. *(Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer)*
**iii.** **`Analytical engine`** (or **`Mark-1`**) was a general purpose, fully program-controlled and automatic mechanical/electromechanical digital computer.
**iv.** **`Pascal's Pascaline calculator`** had a system of gears. One-tooth gear of this machine engages tooth with a ten-tooth gear once every time it revolves. *(Invented by Blaise Pascal in 1642)*
**v.** **`Mark-1`** (or **`UNIVAC`** / **`ENIAC`**) processes data in numerical form using digital circuits.

questions.questionText: How many image files, of size 512 kilobytes each, can be stored on 1500 megabytes of a DVD? Show your working. (2 Marks)
questions.currentSloDescription: distinguish among the memory measuring units such as bits, bytes, kilobytes, megabytes, and gigabytes in computer memory;
questions.sloText: Distinguish among the memory measuring units such as bits, bytes, kilobytes, megabytes, and gigabytes in computer memory;
checkingHints: 1 mark for converting 1500 MB into KB (1500 × 1024 = 1,536,000 KB) or finding 2 files per MB.
1 mark for dividing 1,536,000 / 512 = 3000 files.
questions.overallPerformance: Memory unit conversion questions showed mixed performance where candidates divided without converting MB to KB.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses performed the conversion between kilobytes and megabytes (1500 × 1024 = 1,536,000 KB) and divided by 512 KB to get 3000 files.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses divided 1500 by 512 directly without making the memory units the same (getting 2.9296875 files).
suggestions: Reinforce converting both quantities to the same memory unit (KB) before dividing.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Part a: Number of 512 KB Image Files on a 1500 MB DVD (2 Marks)
1. Convert DVD storage capacity from Megabytes (MB) to Kilobytes (KB):
   $$1\text{ MB} = 1024\text{ KB}$$
   $$1500\text{ MB} = 1500 \times 1024\text{ KB} = 1,536,000\text{ KB}$$
2. Divide total capacity in KB by the size of each image file ($512\text{ KB}$):
   $$\text{Number of files} = \frac{1,536,000\text{ KB}}{512\text{ KB}} = 3000\text{ image files}$$
   *(Alternative method: $1\text{ MB} = 1024\text{ KB}$ holds $\frac{1024}{512} = 2\text{ files per MB}$, so $1500\text{ MB} \times 2 = 3000\text{ files}$.)*

questions.questionText:
Convert the given octal number into decimal number. Show your working. (2 Marks)
$$(65.4)_8$$
questions.sloText: Convert octal numbers (with fractional parts) into decimal numbers;
checkingHints: 1 mark for positional expansion $(6 \times 8^1) + (5 \times 8^0) + (4 \times 8^{-1})$.
1 mark for final decimal value $48 + 5 + 0.5 = 53.5$.
questions.overallPerformance: Octal-to-decimal conversion with a radix point was generally not well attempted.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses used $8^1$ and $8^0$ on the left of the point and $8^{-1}$ on the right of the point to obtain $48 + 5 + 0.5 = 53.5$.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses failed to convert the fractional digit $.4$ using $8^{-1}$ and wrote $(53.4)_{10}$.
suggestions: Practise negative positional powers ($8^{-1}, 2^{-1}$) for fractional base conversions.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Part a: Octal $(65.4)_8$ to Decimal Conversion (2 Marks)
Multiply each octal digit by its positional power of $8$ ($8^1, 8^0$ to the left of the radix point and $8^{-1}$ to the right):
$$(65.4)_8 = (6 \times 8^1) + (5 \times 8^0) + (4 \times 8^{-1})$$
$$(65.4)_8 = (6 \times 8) + (5 \times 1) + \left(4 \times \frac{1}{8}\right)$$
$$(65.4)_8 = 48 + 5 + 0.5 = (53.5)_{10}$$

1.5 marks for converting $(10111011)_2$ into decimal ($128 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 187_{10}$) to prove equality.

checkingHints: 1 mark for defining CLI (user types text commands via keyboard).
1 mark for defining GUI (user interacts visually via icons, menus, windows, and mouse pointer).
questions.overallPerformance: Many candidates wrote comparison features (easy/hard, memory usage) instead of defining what CLI and GUI are.

questions.modelAnswer:
### Part a: Definitions of CLI and GUI (2 Marks)
- **i. Command Line Interface (CLI) (1 Mark):** A text-based user interface in which the user interacts with the operating system by typing explicit **text commands** using a keyboard at a command prompt (e.g., MS-DOS, UNIX shell).
- **ii. Graphical User Interface (GUI) (1 Mark):** A visual user interface in which the user interacts with the computer using graphical elements such as **windows, icons, menus, and a pointing device/mouse (`WIMP`)** (e.g., Microsoft Windows, macOS, Ubuntu Linux).

questions.questionText: Define 'internal' and 'external' commands in DOS and give an example of any ONE of these. (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Define internal and external commands in MS-DOS with examples;
checkingHints: 1.5 marks for defining Internal commands (reside in `COMMAND.COM` / RAM) and External commands (reside as separate `.COM`, `.EXE`, `.BAT` files on disk).
0.5 mark for any ONE valid command example (e.g., `CLS`, `DIR`, `CHKDSK`).
questions.overallPerformance: More candidates succeeded on this knowledge-level DOS question than on application-level command syntax questions.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses defined internal DOS commands as residing in `COMMAND.COM` (e.g., `CLS`) and external DOS commands as requiring separate `.BAT`, `.COM`, or `.EXE` files on disk (e.g., `CHKDSK`).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses wrote tautologies like 'internal commands are used internally and external commands are used externally'.
suggestions: Emphasise the storage location difference: `COMMAND.COM` in RAM (Internal) vs separate executable files on disk (External).
questions.modelAnswer:
### Part b: Internal and External Commands in MS-DOS (2 Marks)
- **Internal Commands:** Commands that are built directly into the **`COMMAND.COM`** command interpreter and loaded into **main memory (RAM)** automatically when the computer boots. They execute immediately without needing a separate disk file.
  - *Examples:* `DIR`, `CLS`, `VER`, `MD`, `CD`, `COPY`, `DEL`, `TIME`, `DATE`.
- **External Commands:** Commands that are NOT built into `COMMAND.COM` in RAM; instead, they reside on secondary storage (hard disk/floppy) as separate executable files (**`.COM`, `.EXE`, or `.BAT`**) and must be loaded from disk when executed.
  - *Examples:* `FORMAT`, `DISKCOPY`, `CHKDSK`, `DELTREE`, `XCOPY`, `EDIT`.

questions.questionText:
i. The given image shows the system bus in a typical computer. Identify **address bus**, **control bus** and **data bus** (`A`, `B`, `C`) on the basis of connections shown among CPU, Memory and Input and Output units of a computer system. (3 Marks)

questions.currentSloDescription: illustrate the system bus and its types, including data bus, address bus and control bus, along with their roles in computer architecture using a diagram;

questions.modelAnswer:
### Part a: Application Software for a Teacher's Routine Tasks (7 Marks)
**i. TWO Application Software for a Teacher (1 Mark — 0.5 Mark Each):**
1. **Spreadsheet Software** *(e.g., Microsoft Excel / Google Sheets)*
2. **Presentation Software** *(e.g., Microsoft PowerPoint)* or **Word Processing Software** *(e.g., Microsoft Word)*

**ii. THREE Uses of Each Identified Software for a Teacher (6 Marks — 3 Marks Each):**
- **Uses of MS Excel (Spreadsheet Software) (3 Marks):**
  1. **Automated Report Cards & Grading:** Using built-in formulas (`SUM`, `AVERAGE`, `IF`, `MIN`, `MAX`) to automatically calculate student totals, percentages, and letter grades without manual calculation errors.
  2. **Attendance Registers:** Maintaining daily/monthly student attendance sheets and automatically computing attendance percentages.
  3. **Class Timetables & Performance Charts:** Organising structured rows and columns for class schedules and generating bar/pie charts to visualise class exam performance.
- **Uses of MS PowerPoint (Presentation Software) (3 Marks):**
  1. **Interactive Multimedia Lectures:** Designing engaging slide decks with diagrams, images, audio/video clips, and animations to explain complex concepts visually.
  2. **Reusable Lesson Plans & Revision Summaries:** Saving structured topic slides that can be updated and reused across academic terms or shared with students.
  3. **Visualising Data & Charts in Class:** Embedding charts, tables, and SmartArt flowcharts to present topic breakdowns clearly on a projector.

questions.questionText:
Utility software is a type of system software used to support the computer infrastructure, distinguishing it from application software which is aimed at directly performing tasks that benefit ordinary users.
Explain the functionality of any FOUR utility software using appropriate examples. (7 Marks)
questions.currentSloDescription: explain the following types of system software: a. operating system, b. device drivers, c. utility programs, d. language processors;
questions.sloText: Explain the following types of system software: a. operating system, b. device drivers, c. utility programs, d. language processors;
checkingHints: 1 mark for naming four valid utility software examples + 1.5 marks each for explaining the functionality of FOUR utility programs (Antivirus, File Compression, Backup, Screen Saver / Disk Cleanup / Defragmenter = 7 Marks).
questions.overallPerformance: Less than 30% of candidates attempted Part (b), and several confused utility programs with application software.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses named four concrete utility programs (e.g., BackupMyPC, WinZip, McAfee Antivirus, Screen Saver) and clearly explained how each maintains, compresses, backs up, or protects the computer.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses listed compilers, DOS, Windows, MS Word, or Photoshop as utility software.
suggestions: Contrast System Software (OS, Device Drivers, Utilities, Language Translators) with Application Software using concrete examples.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Part b: Functionality of FOUR Utility Software with Examples (7 Marks)
1. **Antivirus Software (e.g., McAfee, Norton, Avira, Windows Defender):** Scans hard drives, USB flash drives, and incoming downloads in real time to detect, quarantine, and remove malicious software (viruses, worms, trojans, spyware).
2. **File Compression Utility (e.g., WinZip, WinRAR, 7-Zip):** Compresses large files and folders into smaller archive packages (`.zip`, `.rar`) so they occupy less disk space and can be emailed or transferred faster.
3. **Backup & Recovery Utility (e.g., Windows Backup, BackupMyPC, Acronis):** Creates duplicate copies of important files, databases, and system images on external drives or cloud storage so data can be restored after accidental deletion or hardware failure.
4. **Disk Defragmenter / Disk Cleanup Utility (e.g., Windows Defragmenter, CCleaner):** Reorganises fragmented file clusters contiguously on a magnetic hard disk (and removes temporary junk files) to improve file access speed and free up storage space.
